title: Caracazo Riots
description: On 27 February 1989, nationwide protests, looting, and riots erupted in response to President Carlos Andrés Pérez's IMF-mandated austerity package, which included a 30% rise in public-transport fares and cuts to fuel subsidies. Security forces killed an estimated 276–3,000 people in what became the deadliest civilian unrest in Venezuelan history. The Caracazo shattered the legitimacy of the two-party puntofijista system and radicalized the military officers who later attempted the 1992 coups.

title: February Military Coup Attempt — Chávez's MBR-200
description: On 4 February 1992 Lieutenant Colonel Hugo Chávez led the Revolutionary Bolivarian Movement-200 in a coordinated coup attempt against President Carlos Andrés Pérez. After the coup failed, Chávez's televised 'por ahora' ('for now') concession speech made him a nationally known figure. He was convicted of sedition and imprisoned, but pardoned by President Rafael Caldera in 1994.

title: November Military Coup Attempt
description: On 27 November 1992, a second coup attempt was launched by military officers loyal to the imprisoned Chávez, involving Air Force jets bombing the presidential palace and military units seizing a television station. The uprising was suppressed by loyalist troops; the failed attempt deepened the political crisis of the Pérez government and accelerated calls for constitutional reform.

title: Impeachment of President Carlos Andrés Pérez
description: On 20 May 1993 the Venezuelan Supreme Court found merit in corruption charges against President Carlos Andrés Pérez for embezzlement of 250 million bolívars from a discretionary presidential fund. The Senate stripped him of immunity on 21 May, and Congress removed him permanently from office on 31 August 1993. His 1996 conviction marked the first time a sitting Venezuelan president was impeached and removed.

title: Venezuelan Banking Crisis — Banco Latino Collapse
description: A systemic banking crisis erupted in January 1994 when Banco Latino — the country's second-largest bank — collapsed, triggering a wave of bank failures that wiped out more than 17 financial institutions representing roughly 60% of Venezuela's banking assets. The government spent an estimated 12–15% of GDP on bailouts. New President Rafael Caldera reimposed exchange controls and emergency economic restrictions in an attempt to stem capital flight.

title: Rafael Caldera Re-enters Power — Pardons Chávez
description: Rafael Caldera won the presidency in December 1993 and was inaugurated in February 1994 as an independent, defeating both major establishment parties (AD and COPEI) for the first time in the puntofijista era. In March 1994 Caldera issued pardons to Hugo Chávez and other coup participants of 1992. The pardon was politically controversial but allowed Chávez to transition from jailed coup leader to legitimate political organiser, directly enabling his 1998 electoral rise.

title: Agenda Venezuela Economic Stabilization Package
description: Facing near-hyperinflation and a near-depleted foreign reserve position, President Rafael Caldera reversed course and adopted the IMF-backed 'Agenda Venezuela' structural-adjustment plan in April 1996. The programme liberalized exchange rates, cut fuel subsidies, and partially re-privatized state enterprises. Inflation fell from over 100% in 1996 to around 38% by 1997, temporarily stabilizing the economy before the 1998 oil-price shock.

title: Oil Price Collapse and Economic Crisis
description: Global crude oil prices collapsed to around $10 per barrel in 1998 — their lowest in over a decade — gutting Venezuela's oil-dependent economy. GDP per capita fell to the same level as 1963 in real terms, representing a one-third decline from the 1978 peak. The crisis destroyed confidence in the traditional AD-COPEI party system and propelled the outsider candidate Hugo Chávez to a landslide electoral victory in December 1998.

title: Hugo Chávez Elected President
description: On 6 December 1998 Hugo Chávez won the presidential election with 56% of the vote, defeating Henrique Salas Römer. Running on an anti-corruption, pro-poor platform and promising a constituent assembly, Chávez's victory ended 40 years of political dominance by the AD and COPEI parties and ushered in the Bolivarian Revolution.

title: New Bolivarian Constitution Adopted
description: On 15 December 1999 Venezuelans voted by 72% to ratify a new constitution drafted by a Constituent Assembly dominated by Chávez allies. The constitution renamed the country the 'Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela,' extended the presidential term from 5 to 6 years (renewable once), added a unicameral National Assembly, and expanded social rights. It was the first Venezuelan constitution approved by popular referendum.

title: Chávez Issues 49 Decree-Laws — Business Sector Backlash
description: In November 2001 President Chávez used enabling-law powers to issue 49 decree-laws, including a new Land Reform Law and a new Hydrocarbons Law that increased state royalties and required majority state ownership in oil joint ventures. The business federation Fedecámaras and trade-union confederation CTV declared a national civic strike in December 2001, marking the beginning of a prolonged confrontation between the government and Venezuela's private sector.

title: April Coup Attempt Against Chávez
description: On 11 April 2002 a military coup ousted President Hugo Chávez after security forces fired on pro-government protesters during a massive anti-government march in Caracas, killing at least 19. Business leader Pedro Carmona was briefly installed as president but reversed within 47 hours when loyalist troops and mass popular mobilization restored Chávez to power on 14 April. The United States was later criticized for tacitly endorsing the coup.

title: PDVSA General Strike Begins
description: In December 2002 the opposition, led by Fedecámaras and the CTV, launched a general strike centred on the state oil company PDVSA in an attempt to force Chávez's resignation or a recall referendum. The strike lasted until February 2003, cutting oil production to near zero and costing the economy an estimated $10 billion. After the strike collapsed, Chávez fired approximately 18,000 PDVSA workers — 40% of the workforce — and cemented government control over the company.

title: PDVSA Purge and Misiones Social Programmes Launch
description: After defeating the 2002–03 oil strike, Chávez fired roughly 18,000 PDVSA employees and placed loyalists throughout the company's management, ending its operational independence. Revenues from the re-centralised PDVSA funded a rapid expansion of 'misiones' (social missions): Barrio Adentro (healthcare), Misión Robinson (literacy), Misión Sucre (higher education), and Mercal (subsidised food). World Bank data show Venezuela's poverty rate fell from around 49% in 1998 to 27% by 2007 during the oil boom.

title: Presidential Recall Referendum — Chávez Survives
description: On 15 August 2004 Venezuelans voted in a recall referendum on whether to remove President Chávez from office. Chávez survived with 59% voting 'no' to recall, against the opposition's 41%. Record turnout was observed by the Carter Center and OAS, which certified the result as fair, though the opposition alleged fraud. The result consolidated Chávez's political grip and accelerated oil-financed social programme ('misión') spending.

title: Land Reform Accelerates — Large Estate Expropriations
description: From 2005, Venezuela's Land Reform Law enforcement intensified: the government declared millions of hectares of large privately owned estates ('latifundios') unproductive and subject to expropriation for redistribution to landless peasants. By 2010 the state had redistributed or claimed more than 4 million hectares. The process fueled violent conflicts between landowners and beneficiaries, with hundreds of rural workers killed over the decade.

title: Chávez Re-elected with 63% Majority
description: On 3 December 2006 Hugo Chávez won a third presidential term with a commanding 63% of the vote against opposition candidate Manuel Rosales's 37% — his largest electoral margin. The outcome was widely seen as an endorsement of the Bolivarian social programmes funded by the then-high oil revenues and set the stage for Chávez's accelerated '21st-century socialism' agenda.

title: RCTV Broadcast License Non-Renewal
description: On 27 May 2007 Venezuela's oldest private television network, Radio Caracas Televisión (RCTV), went off air after the government refused to renew its broadcast concession, citing RCTV's support for the 2002 coup. The closure sparked major street protests, particularly among university students, and was condemned by press-freedom organisations worldwide as an attack on free speech. It marked the first large-scale restriction of broadcast media under Chávez.

title: Constitutional Reform Referendum Defeated
description: On 2 December 2007 a package of 69 constitutional amendments championed by Chávez — including indefinite presidential re-election, expanded state control over the economy, and a shortened working day — was narrowly rejected by voters (51% no versus 49% yes). It was the first and only electoral defeat of Chávez's career. The amendments were substantially reintroduced and passed in a subsequent 2009 referendum limited to term limits.

title: ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips Orinoco Nationalizations — ICSID Arbitration
description: After Chávez's 2007 nationalization of Orinoco heavy-oil projects that forced ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips to accept minority stakes, both companies refused and exited Venezuela. ExxonMobil obtained a New York court order briefly freezing PDVSA assets worth $12 billion in early 2008. The disputes proceeded to international arbitration; ConocoPhillips was eventually awarded $8.7 billion by ICSID in 2019. The episodes accelerated capital flight from Venezuela's oil sector.

title: Chávez Nationalizes Cement, Steel, and Banking Sectors
description: Throughout 2008 the Chávez government accelerated nationalizations beyond oil, expropriating major cement producers (CEMEX Venezuela, Holcim, and Lafarge), the steel company SIDOR (from Argentine firm Ternium), and several banks. The government paid compensation below market rates, prompting international arbitration claims. The wave of nationalizations expanded the public sector while reducing private investment in key industries, contributing to supply bottlenecks visible by 2010.

title: Constitutional Referendum Abolishes Presidential Term Limits
description: On 15 February 2009 Venezuela approved a constitutional amendment abolishing term limits for all elected officials by 54% to 46%, allowing President Chávez to seek unlimited re-election. The amendment reversed the single-reelection restriction in the 1999 constitution and was seen as a critical step toward the consolidation of long-term Chávez rule. Voter turnout reached approximately 70%.

title: Energy and Electricity Crisis — First Major Rationing
description: A severe drought in 2009–2010 lowered water levels in the Simón Bolívar hydroelectric plant's reservoir (which provides roughly 70% of Venezuela's electricity) to critically low levels. From January 2010 the government imposed rolling electricity rationing of 9–12 hours per week across most of the country. Chávez declared an electricity emergency and created a Ministry of Electricity. Rationing was lifted in mid-2010 after seasonal rains recovered reservoir levels.

title: Venezuela and Colombia Restore Diplomatic Relations
description: Venezuela broke off diplomatic relations with Colombia in July 2010 after the outgoing Uribe government presented evidence to the OAS that guerrillas from FARC and ELN were operating from Venezuelan territory. Relations were restored within days under newly inaugurated Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos, who signalled a fresh start. The episode illustrated the regional diplomacy tensions inherent in Chávez's support for leftist movements across the continent.

title: Chávez Announces Cancer Diagnosis
description: On 30 June 2011 Hugo Chávez publicly announced he had been diagnosed with cancer after undergoing emergency surgery in Cuba to remove a tumour from his pelvic region. The announcement shocked Venezuela and raised immediate succession questions. Over the following 18 months Chávez underwent multiple surgeries and chemotherapy in Havana while maintaining an active political schedule, including successfully contesting the 2012 presidential election, before his death in March 2013.

title: Chávez Wins Fourth Presidential Term
description: On 7 October 2012 Hugo Chávez defeated opposition candidate Henrique Capriles by 11 percentage points (55% to 44%) to win a fourth presidential term, despite revelations that he was receiving cancer treatment in Cuba. It was his last electoral victory. Chávez died before completing this term; his death on 5 March 2013 triggered a new presidential election.

title: Death of Hugo Chávez
description: Hugo Chávez died on 5 March 2013 at age 58 from respiratory failure following a two-year battle with pelvic cancer. He had governed Venezuela for 14 years and was the dominant figure of the Bolivarian Revolution. Vice President Nicolás Maduro assumed the role of acting president and the country entered a period of national mourning. Chávez's death marked a fundamental shift in Venezuelan politics; his successor would face rapidly deteriorating economic conditions.

title: Nicolás Maduro Wins Snap Presidential Election
description: On 14 April 2013 Nicolás Maduro, Chávez's designated successor, narrowly defeated opposition candidate Henrique Capriles by 1.5 percentage points (50.6% vs. 49.1%) — the closest Venezuelan presidential election in decades. Capriles alleged fraud and demanded a full recount; a partial audit confirmed the result. Maduro's thin margin reflected widespread dissatisfaction and foreshadowed increasingly contested politics.

title: Leopoldo López Arrest — Opposition Leader Imprisoned
description: On 18 February 2014 opposition leader Leopoldo López surrendered to authorities on charges of incitement and conspiracy following nationwide protests he helped organize. In September 2015 he was convicted in proceedings condemned as politically motivated and sentenced to 13 years and 9 months in prison. Amnesty International declared him a prisoner of conscience; the EU and Human Rights Watch demanded his release. He was held in Ramo Verde military prison for three years before transfer to house arrest in 2017.

title: La Salida Anti-Government Protests — 43 Killed
description: Nationwide protests erupted in February 2014, led by opposition leaders Leopoldo López and María Corina Machado, demanding the release of political prisoners and an end to crime and shortages. Security forces and pro-government colectivos killed at least 43 people and detained over 3,000 over four months of unrest. Human Rights Watch documented cases of torture, sexual abuse, and arbitrary detention during the crackdown on demonstrators.

title: Oil Price Collapse Triggers Economic Recession
description: Global Brent crude oil fell from over $100 per barrel in mid-2014 to below $60 by year-end. Since Venezuela depended on oil for approximately 95% of export revenue, the price collapse devastated government finances. GDP contracted 3.9% in 2014, while inflation rose to 69% — the highest in the world at the time. The government refused to devalue the official exchange rate or cut subsidies, accelerating the accumulation of distortions that would produce hyperinflation by 2016.

title: Tren de Aragua Gang Founded in Tocorón Prison
description: The Tren de Aragua criminal organization was founded in 2014 inside the Tocorón prison in Aragua state by Héctor 'El Niño' Guerrero. Operating initially through extortion of construction workers on a nearby railway project, the gang gradually took control of the prison, running internal black markets, a zoo, a disco, and directing violence from behind bars. It later expanded across Latin America and into the United States as Venezuelan migration surged.

title: Opposition Wins National Assembly Supermajority
description: On 6 December 2015 the opposition Democratic Unity Roundtable (MUD) won 112 of 167 National Assembly seats — a two-thirds supermajority — ending 16 years of ruling-party legislative control. The MUD received 7.7 million votes against 5.6 million for the ruling PSUV. Voter turnout reached 74%, the highest for a Venezuelan parliamentary election during the Bolivarian era. The result was seen as a direct rejection of Maduro's management of the economic crisis.

title: Medicine and Hospital Supply Collapse
description: By 2015 Venezuela's health system was experiencing a catastrophic supply shortage, with hospitals reporting up to 95% shortages of essential medicines and 68% shortages of surgical supplies, according to Venezuelan NGO surveys. The Venezuelan Medical Federation reported that 15,000 doctors had left the public health system due to poor pay, drug shortages, and equipment failures. Infant mortality began rising sharply: between 2015 and 2016 infant deaths increased by 30% and maternal deaths by 65%.

title: Hyperinflation Begins — GDP Contracts 18.6%
description: Venezuela officially entered hyperinflation in late 2016, with annual consumer price inflation reaching an estimated 800% by year-end and GDP contracting 18.6%. A humanitarian survey found that 75% of Venezuelans had involuntarily lost an average of 8.7 kg (19 lb) of body weight due to food shortages. The government declared a state of economic emergency in January 2016 and imposed a two-day public-sector work week to conserve electricity during a concurrent drought-driven power crisis.

title: Electricity Crisis and El Niño Drought
description: A powerful El Niño event produced the worst drought in Venezuela in decades, reducing the Guri reservoir (main hydroelectric source) to historically low levels. In April 2016 the government implemented rotating four-hour daily blackouts nationwide, cut the public-sector working week to two days in several states, and closed schools on Fridays to conserve power. The electricity crisis severely disrupted hospitals, factories, and basic services across the country.

title: CLAP Food Box System Introduced Amid Acute Shortages
description: In 2016 the Maduro government launched the CLAP (Local Committees for Supply and Production) programme to distribute subsidised food bags to households as a response to critical shortages. By March 2016, 87% of Venezuelans reported consuming less food. Human rights groups including PROVEA documented that CLAP access was conditioned on political loyalty, constituting a form of food-based political control. By April 2017 over 11% of Venezuelan children under five showed signs of malnutrition.

title: HIV Antiretroviral Shortage — 90% Supply Gap
description: In 2016 Venezuela's antiretroviral (ARV) supply collapsed, with advocacy group Asovida reporting a 90% shortage of HIV medications and warning that over 61,000 people would lose treatment access by mid-year. The broader medicine shortage reached 85% in pharmacies and 95% in hospitals. A 2016 Human Rights Watch report documented HIV patients unable to obtain treatment for months, leading to preventable deterioration and deaths among people living with HIV.

title: Diphtheria Re-emerges After 24-Year Absence
description: In July 2016 Venezuela reported its first diphtheria cases in 24 years, with 183 suspected cases recorded by November 2016 across 16 of Venezuela's 24 federal entities. By 2018 cumulative cases exceeded 2,170. The CDC and PAHO attributed the outbreak to the collapse of routine childhood vaccination, which fell dramatically due to vaccine procurement failures and health system deterioration. The outbreak spread to neighbouring countries via Venezuelan migration.

title: Maduro Dissolves National Assembly — Constitutional Crisis
description: In March–April 2017 the pro-government Supreme Tribunal of Justice (TSJ) issued rulings effectively nullifying the opposition-controlled National Assembly, transferring its powers to itself. Although the rulings were partially walked back under international pressure, Maduro proceeded to announce a Constituent Assembly to replace the parliament. The actions were condemned by the OAS, the US, and EU as an unconstitutional power grab and triggered months of street protests.

title: Mass Anti-Government Protests — 125 Killed
description: From April through July 2017 Venezuela experienced its worst wave of civil unrest since the Caracazo, as millions of citizens protested Maduro's authoritarianism, food shortages, and rising repression. At least 125 people died and over 5,000 were detained over four months. Security forces and pro-government colectivos used live ammunition, rubber bullets, and tear gas against protesters. Human Rights Watch documented systematic torture of detainees during the period.

title: Constituent Assembly Installed — National Assembly Bypassed
description: On 30 July 2017 Venezuela held an election for a National Constituent Assembly (ANC) boycotted by the opposition and widely condemned as fraudulent; the government claimed 8 million voters participated but independent analysts estimated turnout at under 3.7 million. The ANC was inaugurated on 4 August 2017 and assumed supreme legislative powers, effectively sidelining the elected National Assembly. It was recognized only by a handful of governments and marked a decisive shift toward authoritarian rule.

title: Measles Re-emerges — First Confirmed Cases in Decades
description: Measles re-emerged in Venezuela in 2017, with the first confirmed cases in the southern state of Bolívar. From week 26 of 2017 through late 2018, 7,524 suspected cases were reported, of which 6,252 were confirmed (727 in 2017, 5,525 in 2018). The PAHO and CDC attributed the outbreak to collapse of the childhood immunisation programme, with vaccination rates dropping well below the 95% herd immunity threshold. Cases spread to Brazil, Colombia, and Ecuador linked to Venezuelan nationals.

title: Sovereign and PDVSA Bond Default
description: In November 2017 Maduro announced Venezuela would 'restructure' its external debt, but within days S&P declared Venezuela in selective default after missed coupon payments on government and PDVSA bonds. Venezuela and PDVSA's defaulted bonds had a combined face value exceeding $75 billion; total external obligations were estimated at $160–180 billion including accrued interest and arbitration awards. US sanctions effectively blocked any formal restructuring, freezing bondholders in limbo.

title: Trump Financial Sanctions — Executive Order 13808
description: On 24 August 2017 President Trump signed Executive Order 13808, prohibiting US persons from dealing in new debt or equity issued by the Venezuelan government or PDVSA, and blocking dividend payments to the Venezuelan government. The order was issued in response to the installation of the illegitimate Constituent Assembly and documented human rights abuses. The sanctions effectively cut Venezuela off from US capital markets, accelerating the deterioration of PDVSA's finances.

title: CARITAS Reports Acute Child Malnutrition — National Emergency
description: Cáritas Venezuela's sentinel monitoring system reported that moderate and severe acute malnutrition (MAM/SAM) among children under five rose from approximately 10% in early 2017 to 17% by March 2018. A 2018 Cáritas survey found that 21% of pregnant women in low-income communities had moderate or severe acute malnutrition. The findings constituted the first systematically collected evidence of a humanitarian nutrition emergency in Venezuela under international classification standards.

title: Bolivar Soberano Currency Redenomination
description: On 20 August 2018 Venezuela replaced the bolívar fuerte with a new currency, the bolívar soberano, slashing five zeroes from the denomination in an attempt to manage hyperinflation running above 65,000% annually. The redenomination was tied to an anchor linked to the state-issued Petro cryptocurrency and a minimum-wage increase. Economists universally assessed the measure as cosmetic; the IMF projected annual inflation would reach 1.37 million percent by year-end 2018.

title: Petro Cryptocurrency Launch — Sanction-Evasion Attempt
description: Venezuela's Petro cryptocurrency was announced in December 2017 and officially launched in February 2018, backed ostensibly by oil reserves and intended to circumvent US financial sanctions. President Trump signed an executive order in March 2018 prohibiting US persons from transacting in the Petro. Venezuela's own National Assembly declared the Petro an illegal debt issuance. The cryptocurrency failed to achieve meaningful adoption and was terminated by the Venezuelan government in January 2024.

title: Juan Requesens Arrested — Alleged Drone Assassination Plot
description: On 7 August 2018, three days after two explosives-laden drones detonated near a military parade where Maduro was speaking, opposition National Assembly deputy Juan Requesens was arrested and imprisoned in El Helicoide. The government broadcast a video alleged to be a confession, though Requesens never mentioned the drone attack. Human rights organizations documented torture during his detention. He was sentenced to eight years in 2022 and released to house arrest before that verdict.

title: Maduro Re-elected in Disputed Vote
description: On 20 May 2018 Nicolás Maduro was re-elected with a claimed 68% of the vote in an election widely condemned as fraudulent. The main opposition coalition boycotted the poll, and turnout fell to around 46% — the lowest in decades. The United States, European Union, Lima Group, and OAS Secretary-General refused to recognize the results. The US imposed additional sanctions targeting Venezuelan oil revenues following the election.

title: EU Sanctions Seven Senior Officials — Diosdado Cabello Among Targets
description: On 18 January 2018 the European Union imposed targeted sanctions — asset freezes and travel bans — on seven senior Venezuelan officials including Diosdado Cabello (PSUV president), Interior Minister Néstor Reverol, Intelligence Chief Gustavo González López, and four others. The sanctions cited responsibility for human rights violations, undermining democracy, and blocking humanitarian assistance. The EU continued renewing and expanding these individual sanctions in subsequent years.

title: Guaidó Declares Himself Interim President
description: On 23 January 2019 National Assembly president Juan Guaidó invoked constitutional provisions to declare himself Venezuela's interim president in front of hundreds of thousands of supporters at a Caracas rally. Within hours, the United States recognized Guaidó, followed by approximately 50 other countries including most of the EU and the Lima Group. Maduro retained control of the military, state institutions, and Cuba-backed intelligence services, creating a dual-authority standoff that persisted until 2022.

title: US Treasury Full Oil Sector Sanctions on PDVSA
description: On 28 January 2019 the US Treasury Department imposed comprehensive sanctions on PDVSA, Venezuela's state oil company, freezing approximately $7 billion in assets and blocking $11 billion in projected revenue over the following year. The sanctions were intended to deprive the Maduro government of oil income while excluding humanitarian exemptions. PDVSA exports shifted to Russia, China, and Cuba, but oil production — already declining — fell further, reaching record lows under 700,000 bpd by 2020.

title: Nationwide Blackouts — Longest Power Failure in Modern Venezuelan History
description: On 7 March 2019 Venezuela suffered a catastrophic nationwide electricity blackout that lasted up to seven days in some regions, caused by a failure at the Simón Bolívar (Guri) hydroelectric plant amid alleged cyberattack claims by the Maduro government. Hospitals operated on generators; doctors reported surges in diarrhea, typhoid, and hepatitis A. Multiple shorter blackouts followed through April 2019. The crisis exposed the total collapse of electricity infrastructure after years of underinvestment.

title: Failed April 30 Military Uprising — Operation Freedom
description: On 30 April 2019 Juan Guaidó and Leopoldo López (freed from house arrest by defecting officers) appeared alongside a small group of armed forces at La Carlota air base calling on the military to defect. Despite prior claims of high-level military commitments, senior commanders remained loyal to Maduro. The uprising collapsed within hours; López sought asylum at the Spanish embassy. Four people were killed in clashes between protesters and pro-government forces.

title: Russia and Cuba Deploy Military Advisers — Wagner Group Reports
description: In January–March 2019, during the height of the Guaidó recognition crisis, Russia deployed approximately 99 troops and 35 tonnes of military materiel to Venezuela, and Wagner Group private military contractors were reported to have arrived to provide security for Maduro. Cuba maintained several thousand intelligence and security advisers embedded in Venezuelan institutions. The allied foreign support was credited by analysts as a key reason Maduro's military did not defect during the 2019 crisis.

title: Bank of England Freezes $1.95 Billion Venezuelan Gold Reserves
description: In early 2019, following UK recognition of Juan Guaidó as interim president, the Bank of England refused requests by the Maduro-appointed Central Bank board to repatriate approximately $1.95 billion (31 tonnes) of Venezuelan gold held in London. The ensuing legal dispute lasted years, with courts alternately ruling in favour of Guaidó- and Maduro-appointed boards. The frozen gold reserves left Venezuela unable to liquidate a key external asset amid comprehensive US sanctions.

title: US Indicts Maduro on Narco-Terrorism Charges — $15M Reward
description: On 26 March 2020 the US Department of Justice unsealed an indictment charging President Nicolás Maduro and five co-defendants with narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, and weapons offences, alleging coordination with FARC to traffic hundreds of tonnes of cocaine through Venezuela. The State Department offered a $15 million reward for information leading to Maduro's arrest. The indictment formally designated Venezuela's Cartel de los Soles as a narco-state structure.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic Deepens Humanitarian Crisis
description: Venezuela reported its first confirmed COVID-19 case on 13 March 2020. Maduro imposed strict quarantine measures and used the pandemic to intensify repression of dissent and restrict opposition activities. The health system — already near-collapsed with 80% of hospitals lacking basic supplies — struggled to respond. PAHO estimated Venezuela had only one ventilator per 100 ICU beds. The pandemic accelerated emigration and deepened food and medicine shortages already affecting 96% of the population.

title: Venezuela Migration Crisis Reaches 5.4 Million
description: By 2021 an estimated 5.4 million Venezuelans — nearly 20% of the country's population — had emigrated, making the Venezuelan diaspora the second-largest displacement crisis in the world after Syria. Colombia alone hosted over 1.7 million Venezuelan refugees. UNHCR reported that push factors included hyperinflation, food and medicine shortages, insecurity, and political persecution. The International Organization for Migration designated Venezuela's migration as a 'regional emergency.'

title: Regional Elections — Opposition Wins Several Governorships
description: In regional elections on 21 November 2021 the opposition won important governorships including Cojedes, Nueva Esparta, Anzoátegui, and Barinas, the home state of Hugo Chávez. The ruling PSUV retained 20 of 23 governorships overall, but the opposition's gains — particularly in Barinas — were symbolically significant and demonstrated that competitive elections remained possible in some districts despite structural advantages for the government.

title: Guaidó's Interim Government Dissolved — Opposition Restructures
description: In December 2022 Venezuela's opposition-dominated National Assembly voted to dissolve Juan Guaidó's interim government, ending a nearly four-year dual-authority standoff. The United States formally stopped recognizing Guaidó's presidential claim in January 2023. The opposition restructured under a Unitary Platform coalition, began negotiating with the Maduro government in Barbados, and eventually rallied behind Edmundo González Urrutia as its 2024 presidential candidate.

title: Chevron Licence Restored — Partial Easing of US Oil Sanctions
description: In November 2022 the Biden administration issued a limited licence allowing Chevron Corporation to resume oil-for-debt swap operations in Venezuela for the first time since 2019. This represented the first significant US sanctions relief during the Maduro era, conditioned on progress in Venezuelan government-opposition talks in Mexico City. Chevron's return modestly increased oil production and provided PDVSA with foreign exchange, though output remained far below pre-sanctions levels.

title: Barbados Agreement — Maduro Government and Opposition Sign Election Roadmap
description: In October 2023 the Venezuelan government and the opposition Unitary Platform signed the Barbados Agreement, committing to conditions for free and fair presidential elections including release of political prisoners and re-registration of political parties. In exchange the Biden administration eased sanctions on Venezuela's oil, gas, and gold sectors. The agreement raised international hopes for a democratic transition, though the government subsequently reneged on key provisions in 2024.

title: Venezuelan Diaspora Reaches 7.7 Million — Largest in Latin America
description: By November 2023 UNHCR and the R4V coordination platform estimated that 7.7 million Venezuelans had left the country, representing over 25% of the population — the largest exodus in Latin America's recent history. Colombia (2.9 million) and Peru (1.5 million) hosted the largest numbers. Over 520,000 Venezuelans crossed the Darién Gap between Panama and Colombia in 2023 alone, with Venezuelans comprising approximately 60% of all Darién crossings that year.

title: María Corina Machado Disqualified from Presidential Race
description: On 30 June 2023 Venezuela's Comptroller General disqualified opposition leader María Corina Machado from holding public office for 15 years, alleging links to the Guaidó government and support for international sanctions. Despite the ban, Machado won the opposition primary in October 2023 with over 90% of the vote. The Supreme Tribunal of Justice upheld the disqualification in January 2024, violating the Barbados Agreement commitment to permit opposition participation.

title: Tareck El Aissami Arrested for PdVSA Corruption
description: On 9 April 2024 Venezuela's attorney general announced the arrest of former Vice President and Oil Minister Tareck El Aissami alongside businessman Samark López Bello, accused of leading a scheme that illicitly sold PdVSA crude shipments without the proceeds reaching state coffers — the so-called PdVSA-Cripto corruption network. El Aissami had previously been sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2017 for drug trafficking through Venezuela's Cartel de los Soles. His arrest represented an extraordinary intra-regime prosecution.

title: Presidential Election Fraud — Maduro Declared Winner Despite Evidence of González Victory
description: On 28 July 2024 Venezuela held a presidential election between Nicolás Maduro and opposition candidate Edmundo González. The National Electoral Council declared Maduro the winner without publishing booth-level tallies. The opposition gathered verified tallies from 80% of voting machines showing González won by a wide margin. The Carter Center, OAS, United Nations, and most Western governments refused to recognise the official results. At least 22 people were killed in post-election protests.

title: Operation Tun Tun — Mass Post-Election Arrests
description: Following the disputed 28 July 2024 election, the Maduro government launched 'Operation Tun Tun,' a door-to-door sweep that detained more than 2,000 people — including protesters, civil society leaders, and relatives of opposition activists — within weeks. Arrest warrants were issued for opposition candidate Edmundo González; he fled to asylum in Spain on 7 September 2024. Human rights organisations documented torture, arbitrary detention, and enforced disappearances during the crackdown.

title: Post-Election Protests — Security Forces Kill Demonstrators
description: Following the disputed July 28, 2024 election result, protests erupted across Venezuela in dozens of cities. Security forces, National Guard units, and pro-government colectivos responded with lethal force; at least 22 protesters were killed and over 1,500 detained in the first weeks. The UN Human Rights Office called for an independent investigation and documented widespread arbitrary detention. Opposition leaders and civil society figures were arrested in what OHCHR described as a systematic campaign of repression.

title: Maduro Inaugurated for Third Term Amid International Condemnation
description: On 10 January 2025 Nicolás Maduro was inaugurated for a third presidential term despite the disputed election outcome. The United States, European Union, and approximately 20 Latin American governments refused to recognise the result. Simultaneously, the US reimposed broad oil sanctions and offered a $25 million reward for information leading to Maduro's arrest on narco-terrorism charges. Venezuelan security forces maintained a severe crackdown on dissent into 2025.

title: Venezuela Launches Simon Bolivar, Its First Satellite
description: Venezuela's first satellite, VENESAT-1 (Simon Bolivar), launched aboard a Chinese Long March 3B rocket from Xichang on 29 October 2008. Built on a Chinese DFH-4 bus and operated by Venezuela's Bolivarian Agency for Space Activities, the 5,049kg satellite carried 14 C-band, 12 Ku-band and 2 Ka-band transponders to provide television broadcasting and broadband connectivity until it failed in orbit in March 2020.

title: Venezuela Creates Orinoco Mining Arc Opening Forests to Mining
description: On February 24, 2016, President Nicolas Maduro signed Decree 2,248, creating the Orinoco Mining Arc, a 111,843-square-kilometer 'National Strategic Development Zone' covering 12 percent of Venezuela's territory for large-scale gold, coltan, diamond, and bauxite mining. The decree was issued without National Assembly approval or the environmental impact assessments and indigenous consultations required by the constitution. Within four years, over 2,821 square kilometers of forest were destroyed, half of it inside legally protected territories.
